```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(geosphere)
set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw())
```

## 0. Prepare the data

Problems 1 and 2 use the same Exide soil core data and property covariates as HW2, found in `/courses/EDS222/data`. The code below is provided for you. It's the same as HW2, with one new column: `hazard`.

A soil lead concentration is only a number until someone has to decide what to do about it. In 2024, the US EPA lowered its screening level for lead in residential soil to **200 ppm**. Properties above the screening level get a closer look, and possibly cleanup. In this homework, you'll model the **probability** that a property's average soil lead is at or above the screening level.

The code creates a data frame called `properties` with **one row per property** and the following columns:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `property_id` | Unique property identifier |
| `area` | Sampling area (`"ENA"`, `"ESA"`, or `"SS"`), taken from the first characters of `property_id` |
| `pb_ppm` | Average soil lead concentration across all the property's soil cores (ppm) |
| `hazard` | 1 if `pb_ppm` is at or above the EPA screening level (200 ppm), 0 otherwise |
| `dist_exide_km` | Distance from the former Exide facility (km) |
| `year_built` | Year the home was built |
| `home_age` | Age of the home in 2026 (years) |

```{r}
#| label: prepare-data
#| message: false

data_dir <- "/courses/EDS222/data"

# Approximate location of the former Exide facility (2700 S Indiana St, Vernon)
exide_lon <- -118.1923
exide_lat <- 34.0058

# EPA residential soil lead screening level (ppm)
screening_ppm <- 200

# Load soil cores, drop extreme outliers, and calculate distance to Exide.
soil_cores <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "exide-soil-cores.csv")) |>
  filter(pb_ppm <= 5e3) |>
  mutate(
    area = str_remove(str_sub(property_id, 1, 3), "-"),
    dist_exide_km = distGeo(
      cbind(longitude, latitude),
      c(exide_lon, exide_lat)
    ) / 1000
  )

property_covariates <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "exide-property-covariates.csv"))

# Average the soil cores within each property, then join the covariates.
# Ten properties have no year_built, so drop them.
properties <- soil_cores |>
  summarize(
    pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm),
    dist_exide_km = mean(dist_exide_km),
    .by = c(property_id, area)
  ) |>
  left_join(property_covariates, by = "property_id") |>
  mutate(
    home_age = 2026 - year_built,
    hazard = ifelse(pb_ppm >= screening_ppm, 1, 0)
  ) |>
  drop_na(home_age) |>
  select(property_id, area, pb_ppm, hazard, dist_exide_km, year_built, home_age)

# Check: you should have 314 properties
nrow(properties)
```

## 1. Logistic regression with one predictor

### Scenario

In HW2, you found that soil lead increased with home age. Homes built before 1978 were often painted with lead-based paint, and older homes had more decades of it chipping and weathering into the soil. A resident living in a 100-year-old home asks:

> How likely is it that my soil is above the EPA screening level?

In this problem, you'll answer that question using home age as the only predictor.

### 1a. Visualize the raw data

With a binary response, the raw data are hard to read. Group properties into 10-year bins of home age, then calculate the proportion of properties above the screening level in each bin.

::: {.callout-tip}

`cut()` converts a continuous variable into bins, like you did in lab 7. Home ages range from 27 to 121 years, so bins from 20 to 130 years cover all the properties.

:::

```{r}
#| label: age-bins

properties <- properties |>
  mutate(
    age_bin = cut(home_age, breaks = seq(20, 130, by = 10), include.lowest = TRUE)
  )

age_summary <- properties |>
  summarize(
    home_age = mean(home_age),
    prop_hazard = mean(hazard),
    n = n(),
    .by = age_bin
  ) |>
  arrange(age_bin)
age_summary
```

Plot the raw data (jittered) with the binned proportions on top. Size the binned points by the number of properties in each bin.

```{r}
#| label: plot-age-hazard

ggplot(properties, aes(x = home_age, y = hazard)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0),
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = prop_hazard, size = n),
    data = age_summary,
    color = "cornflowerblue"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Home age (years)",
    y = "Above screening level",
    size = "Properties"
  )
```

Describe the relationship between home age and the probability that a property is above the screening level. Which bins have too few properties to say much?

As home age increases,

### 1b. Fit the model

Our model in statistical notation is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Hazard} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
\text{logit}(p) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Age}
\end{aligned}
$$

Fit a logistic regression with `hazard` as the response and `home_age` as the predictor.

```{r}
#| label: fit-age-glm

age_glm <- glm(
  hazard ~ home_age,
  family = binomial(link = 'logit'),
  data = properties
)
summary(age_glm)
```

Fill in the blanks to interpret the slope in a complete sentence, including units.

> For every additional year of home age, the **log odds** of soil lead above the screening level **increase** by 0.031.

Fill in the blanks below to interpret the slope's p-value.

$H_0$: the slope = 0, home age has no effect on the log odds that a property is above the screening level

$H_A$: the slope != 0, home age has an effect on the log odds that a property is above the screening level

With a p-value of 4.32e-05, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude there is evidence for $H_A$, that home age has an effect on the log odds that a property is above the screening level.

### 1c. Convert log odds to probabilities

Log odds aren't very intuitive. Create a prediction grid covering the range of home ages in the data, then use `predict()` to get the probability that a property is above the screening level.

```{r}
#| label: predict-age

age_grid <- tibble(
  home_age = seq(min(20), max(130), by = 1)
)
age_grid$p_hazard <- predict(
  age_glm,
  newdata = age_grid,
  type = "response"
)
```

Overlay the predicted probabilities on your figure from 1a.

```{r}
#| label: plot-age-predictions

# Copy your figure from 1a here, then add a geom_line() layer for the predictions

ggplot(properties, aes(x = home_age, y = hazard)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0),
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = prop_hazard, size = n),
    data = age_summary,
    color = "cornflowerblue"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(x = home_age, y = p_hazard),
    data = age_grid,
    color = 'firebrick'
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Home age (years)",
    y = "Above screening level",
    size = "Properties"
  )
```

What does the model predict for the resident's 100-year-old home?

```{r}
#| label: predict-100

predict(
  age_glm,
  newdata = tibble(home_age = 100),
  type = "response"
)
```

The probability that a 100 year old property is above the screening level is predicted by the model to be about 58%. 

### 1d. A constant slope, a changing effect

On the log odds scale, every additional year of home age has the same effect. On the probability scale, it doesn't. Use your model to calculate the change in probability for two 10-year increases in home age: from 30 to 40 years, and from 100 to 110 years.

```{r}
#| label: probability-differences

p_age <- predict(
  age_glm,
  newdata = tibble(home_age = c(30, 40, 100, 110)),
  type = "response"
)
p_age

# Change from 30 to 40 years
0.1741555 - 0.1337357 
# Answer: 0.04

# Change from 100 to 110 years
0.6517213 - 0.5780435 
# Answer: 0.07
```

Both changes are 10 years. Why aren't the changes in probability the same? Use your figure from 1c to explain.

The changes in probability aren't the same because unlike the log odds scale (which is linear and goes between -inf and inf), the probability scale is not linear, it is compressed into an S-curve between 0 and 1.

## 2. Logistic regression with multiple predictors

### Scenario

Home age isn't the only thing that differs among these properties. Exide emitted lead into the air, so you might expect properties closer to the facility to be more likely to exceed the screening level. The three sampling areas also differ in their direction from the facility, their street layouts, and their land uses. If older homes tend to be closer to Exide, or concentrated in one area, then some of the home age effect from problem 1 might belong to distance or area instead.

Your question is:

> After accounting for distance from Exide and sampling area, is an older home more likely to have soil lead above the screening level?

The model has two continuous predictors (`home_age` and `dist_exide_km`) and one categorical predictor with three levels (`area`). As in HW2, ENA is the reference level, and `area` needs two dummy variables:

- $\text{ESA} = 1$ if the property is in ESA, 0 otherwise
- $\text{SS} = 1$ if the property is in SS, 0 otherwise

Here's the model in statistical notation, with $\beta_1$ for home age, $\beta_2$ for distance, and $\beta_3$ and $\beta_4$ for the area dummies.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Hazard} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \\
\text{logit}(p) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Age} + \beta_2 \text{Dist} + \beta_3 \text{ESA} + \beta_4 \text{SS}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 2a. Fit the model

```{r}
#| label: fit-hazard-glm

hazard_glm <- glm(
  hazard ~ home_age + dist_exide_km + area,
  family = binomial(link = 'logit'),
  data = properties
)
summary(hazard_glm)
```

Interpret the coefficients for `home_age` and `dist_exide_km` in complete sentences, including units. Remember that each coefficient describes the effect of that predictor _holding the other predictors constant_. Use the p-values to determine if the estimates are significantly different than 0.

The `home_age` coefficient is 0.03, meaning that with all other variables held constant, for each additional year in home age, the log odds that the property is above the screening level increases by 0.03. The p-value for this coefficient is statistically significant at 0.0002 (less than an alpha significance level of 0.05), meaning that that we have sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis (beta_1 = 0) and have evidence to support the HA (beta_1 != 0, that home age has an impact on the log odds of a property being above the screening level)

The `dist_exide_km` coefficient is -0.64, meaning that with all other variables held constant, for each additional km in distance from exide, the log odds that the property is above the screening level decreases by -0.64. However, the p-value for this coefficient is 0.15, which is greater than an alpha significance level of 0.05, meaning that this coefficient estimate is not statistically significant and we don't have sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis (beta_2 = 0, that distance from exide does not have an impact on the log odds of a property being above the screening level).

Compare the `home_age` coefficient to the one from `age_glm` in problem 1. Did accounting for distance and area change your conclusion about home age?

The coefficients for both models are very similar (both round to 0.03), so accounting for distance and area did not change our conclusion about home age. 

### 2b. Visualize the predictions

With more than one predictor, a prediction grid needs a value for _every_ predictor. Create a grid with every combination of home age (across its range) and area, holding distance from Exide at its median. Then predict the probability for each row of the grid.

::: {.callout-tip}

`expand_grid()` creates a data frame with every combination of the values you give it, like you did in lab 7. If you give it a single value (like the median distance), every row gets that value.

:::

```{r}
#| label: predict-hazard

hazard_grid <- expand_grid(
  home_age = seq(min(20), max(130), by = 1),
  area = c("ENA", "ESA", "SS"),
  dist_exide_km = median(properties$dist_exide_km)
)
hazard_grid$p_hazard <- predict(
  hazard_glm,
  newdata = hazard_grid,
  type = "response"
)
```

Plot the predicted probabilities as one line per area, on top of the jittered raw data colored by area.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hazard-predictions

ggplot(properties, aes(x = home_age, y = hazard, color = area)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0),
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = p_hazard),
    data = hazard_grid,
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Home age (years)",
    y = "Above screening level",
    color = "Sampling area"
  )
```

What does the model predict for a 100-year-old home at the median distance from Exide in each area?

```{r}
#| label: predict-100-area

predict(
  hazard_glm,
  newdata = tibble(
    home_age = 100,
    area = c("ENA", "ESA", "SS"),
    dist_exide_km = median(properties$dist_exide_km)
  ),
  type = "response"
)
```

The model predicts:
ENA: 0.6937402 
ESA: 0.5446699
SS: 0.5601194 

### 2c. Interpret

Answer the following questions in 2-3 sentences each.

1. Based on your model, what would you tell the resident with the 100-year-old home? Use your predictions from 2b.

Based on this model, I would tell the resident with the 100-year-old home that, once distance from the Exide plant is held constant at its median level, homes in the ENA area are estimated to have a 69% probability of having soil lead above the screening level. This is a higher probability than that of the homes in ESA and SS areas, with 54% and 56%, respectively.   

2. The `dist_exide_km` coefficient was not significantly different from 0. Does that mean Exide didn't contaminate these neighborhoods? Think about the range of distances in the data and what the hypothesis test can and can't tell you.

No, this does not conclusively mean that Exide didn't contaminate these neighborhoods. This result just implies that there is not enough evidence to suggest that `dist_exide_km` has a statistically significant effect on the probability of a home having soil lead above the screening level in this dataset. A larger sample size across a wider range of distances (specifically including distances closer the plant) might yield different results - the current data only has homes between 1.2km and 3km from the plant.

## 3. Simulate data for a Poisson regression

### Scenario

Before it closed in 2015, the Exide facility released lead into the air, and regulators monitored the air around the facility for lead. Suppose an air quality agency places lead monitors at different distances from a facility like Exide. Each monitor records the number of days in a year that its daily lead measurement exceeds a health-based threshold. Lead emissions disperse as they travel away from the source, so you'd expect monitors farther from the facility to record fewer exceedance days.

The number of exceedance days is a count, so you'll use a Poisson regression. In this problem, you'll simulate exceedance days for a set of monitors, fit a Poisson regression to your simulated data, and check how well the model recovers the parameters you used.

The model is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Days} &\sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda) \\
\log(\lambda) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Dist}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{Dist}$ is the monitor's distance from the facility (km).

### 3a. Choose your parameters

Before you write code, decide what each parameter means in this scenario and what sign it should have. Fill in the table.

::: {.callout-tip}

The coefficients are on the log scale. Exponentiate them to think about their effects on the expected count.

- $e^{\beta_0}$ is the expected number of exceedance days for a monitor at the facility (distance = 0).
- $e^{\beta_1}$ is the factor that multiplies the expected number of exceedance days for each additional kilometer from the facility. For example, $\beta_1 = -0.5$ means each kilometer multiplies the expected count by $e^{-0.5} = 0.61$, a 39% decrease.

Keep your values realistic. A year has 365 days, and even a monitor next to a major source shouldn't exceed the threshold on most of them. You'll simulate monitors between 0 and 5 km from the facility.

:::

| Parameter | Meaning in this scenario | Sign (+ or -) | Your value |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\beta_0$ | natural log of the expected number of exceedance days for a monitor at the facility (distance = 0) | + | ln(42 days) = 3.7 |
| $\beta_1$ | natural log of the factor that multiplies the expected number of exceedance days for each additional kilometer from the facility | - | ln(0.7) = -0.36 | 

Assuming that the facility was operating year round, it seemed reasonable to expect that 42 days (about 6 cumulative weeks) of the year would have elevated lead levels observed in the air. I selected -0.36 for my beta_1 (corresponds to e^-0.36 = 0.7) because it seems reasonable to expect a moderate decrease (in this case, 30%) in exceedance days as distance from facility increases. 

```{r}
#| label: sim-params

beta_0 <- 3.7
beta_1 <- -0.36
```

### 3b. Simulate the predictor

Simulate `N = 100` monitors. Distance from the facility should be continuous, so use `runif()`.

```{r}
#| label: sim-predictor

N <- 100
dist_km <- runif(N, min = 0, max = 5)
```

### 3c. Simulate the response

First, calculate the expected number of exceedance days ($\lambda$) using your model equation. The model is linear on the _log_ scale, so you'll need to exponentiate. Then simulate the counts with `rpois()`.

```{r}
#| label: sim-response

lambda <- exp(beta_0 + beta_1 * dist_km)
days <- rpois(n = N, lambda = lambda)

simulated_monitors <- tibble(
  dist_km,
  days
)
```

### 3d. Fit the model

Fit a Poisson regression to your simulated data. Then compare the estimated coefficients to the parameters you chose, on both the log scale and the multiplicative scale.

```{r}
#| label: sim-fit

sim_glm <- glm(
  days ~ dist_km,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = simulated_monitors
)
summary(sim_glm)

tibble(
  parameter = c("beta_0", "beta_1"),
  true = c(beta_0, beta_1),
  estimated = coef(sim_glm),
  true_multiplier = exp(c(beta_0, beta_1)),
  estimated_multiplier = exp(coef(sim_glm))
)
```

Interpret the estimated effect of distance in a complete sentence, using the multiplier ($e^{\hat\beta_1}$) rather than the log-scale coefficient. Did the model recover your parameters? Use the standard errors to decide whether the differences between the true and estimated values are larger than you'd expect from chance.

The estimated beta_1 multiplier value (0.705), means that each additional kilometer multiplies the expected number of exceedance days by 0.705, which would mean a 30% decrease in expected exceedance days per kilometer. This model recovered my parameters almost exactly, there is very little difference between the true and estimated values.

### 3e. Visualize the simulation

Make a figure with three layers:

1. The simulated data as points
2. A **dashed** curve for the _true_ relationship (from the $\beta$s you chose)
3. A **solid** curve for the _estimated_ relationship (from `sim_glm`)

In HW2, you drew straight lines with `geom_abline()`. On the count scale, a Poisson regression makes a _curve_, so instead you'll calculate both curves over a prediction grid. Calculate the true curve with your $\beta$s, and the estimated curve with `predict()`.

```{r}
#| label: sim-curves

sim_grid <- tibble(
  dist_km = seq(0, 5, by = 0.05)
)
sim_grid$true_lambda <- exp(beta_0 + beta_1 * sim_grid$dist_km)
sim_grid$estimated_lambda <- predict(
  sim_glm,
  newdata = sim_grid,
  type = "response"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-plot

ggplot(simulated_monitors, aes(x = dist_km, y = days)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = true_lambda),
    data = sim_grid,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1,
    color = "cornflowerblue"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = estimated_lambda),
    data = sim_grid,
    linetype = "solid",
    linewidth = 1,
    color = "firebrick",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Distance from facility (km)",
    y = "Exceedance days per year"
  )
```
